New to the Pokémon TCG? Start Here.

I get asked “how do I even start playing” more than almost anything else — way more than card values, honestly. So here it is: everything you need to sit down with a friend and actually play a full game, no prior knowledge assumed. I’m keeping this to the physical/paper game (Pokémon TCG Live works the same way, just automated). A video version is coming once I’ve got this written version locked down.

The goal

You win one of three ways:

Take all your Prize cards. You set aside 6 cards face-down at the start of the game. Every time you knock out one of your opponent’s Pokémon, you take one (some Pokémon — like ex or VMAX cards — are worth 2 Prize cards when knocked out, so those trade fast).

Your opponent runs out of Pokémon. No Pokémon in play, none left to play — game over.

Your opponent can’t draw a card. If someone’s deck is empty on their draw step, they lose right there. This barely ever comes up, but it exists.

Most games end on Prize cards. Just remember: bigger, splashier Pokémon usually cost your opponent more Prizes when they go down, which matters a lot when you’re deciding what to attack into.

What’s in a deck

60 cards, always. Three types: Pokémon cards — what you actually play and attack with. Trainer cards — Items, Supporters, Stadiums, and Tools, doing everything from drawing extra cards to searching your deck to healing damage. Energy cards — attach these to power up your Pokémon’s attacks.

You can only run 4 copies of any card with the same name (max 4 Pikachu, max 4 Ultra Ball, etc.) — the one exception is basic Energy, which you can run as many of as you want. There are 8 basic Energy types, and there’s no dedicated Colorless Energy card — Colorless costs in attacks can be paid with any Energy type:

Grass
Fire
Water
Lightning
Psychic
Fighting
Dark
Steel

Setting up

Both players shuffle, draw 7 cards, and set a Basic Pokémon face-down as their Active Pokémon (the one doing the fighting) — you can also place more Basics face-down on your Bench, up to 5. Once both players are ready, flip everything face-up, set aside your 6 Prize cards, and you’re in.

Whoever goes first is decided however you like — coin flip, rock-paper-scissors, doesn’t matter.

How a turn works

Every turn has three parts, always in this order:

1. Draw. Draw one card. Mandatory, no skipping it.

2. Main phase. Do as much or as little of this as you want, in any order: play Basic Pokémon to your Bench (up to 5 total); evolve a Pokémon that’s been in play since the start of this turn (you can’t evolve something the same turn you played it); attach one Energy card from your hand to any of your Pokémon (one attachment per turn, total — not per Pokémon); use Pokémon Abilities; play as many Item cards as you want; play one Supporter card; play one Stadium card; retreat your Active Pokémon once, paying its Retreat Cost in Energy, to swap in a Benched Pokémon.

3. Attack. Pick an attack your Active Pokémon has enough Energy for, resolve it, and your turn ends. One attack per turn, and once you attack, that’s it.

The one rule that trips everyone up: the player going first draws a card like normal, but cannot attack and cannot play a Supporter card on their very first turn. Nobody can evolve on turn 1 either, for either player, since evolving needs a Pokémon that’s already been in play since the start of the turn. It sounds fiddly written out, but at the table it just means: turn 1, you set up your board and pass. That’s it.

Standard format and rotation, explained simply

If you’re buying singles or building a tournament-legal deck, you need to know about rotation. Every card released has a small letter printed on it — the regulation mark — usually near the artist credit or set symbol. Once a year, the oldest regulation marks get rotated out of the Standard format, so the format keeps refreshing instead of accumulating years of cards.

The current rotation took effect this year — regulation mark G and everything older is no longer Standard-legal, and only cards marked H and onward are tournament-legal in Standard. Practically, that means anything from Twilight Masquerade onward is safe to build around, and anything from the original Scarlet & Violet base set through Paradox Rift just rotated out. New sets keep adding new regulation marks as they release, and each stays legal until it’s old enough to rotate out in turn.

If you’re just playing casually with friends, none of this matters — play with whatever cards you own. It only bites you if you’re building for an actual Standard tournament.

What’s next

That’s genuinely enough to sit down and play a full game. Once you’re comfortable with the basics, check out my Meta Decks page for what’s actually winning right now, or Jack’s Decks if you want to see what I personally play. And if you want to play an actual game with me — in person here in Singapore, or on Pokémon TCG Live — head to Play with Jack.

Written by Jack, cross-referenced against the official tournament rules and a handful of community rules guides — if anything here ever looks off, tell me and I’ll fix it.

Deck spotlight: Mega Excadrill ex

Currently the single most-played deck in Standard. It’s a Metal-type control list — Beldum into Metang into Metagross forms the engine, Drilbur digs for Mega Excadrill ex, and Genesect ex backs it up. Here’s a real 60-card list from a recent major (credit to competitor AzulGG):

Pokémon · 20

  • 4 Beldum TEF 113
  • 4 Metang TEF 114
  • 2 Metagross CRI 61
  • 4 Drilbur PBL 46
  • 2 Mega Excadrill ex PBL 65
  • 2 Genesect ex BLK 67
  • 1 Fezandipiti ex ASC 142
  • 1 Mega Skarmory ex POR 55

Trainer · 23

  • 4 Brock’s Scouting
  • 4 Team Rocket’s Petrel
  • 4 Buddy-Buddy Poffin
  • 2 Jumbo Ice Cream
  • 2 Team Rocket’s Transceiver
  • 1 Switch
  • 1 Energy Recycler
  • 1 Ultra Ball
  • 1 Pokégear 3.0
  • 1 Tool Scrapper
  • 1 Hero’s Cape
  • 1 Gravity Mountain

Energy · 17

  • 17 Metal Energy

Learn At BlackLabel TCG

A completely unpaid, unsponsored shoutout for a shop and a community I genuinely love.

Full disclosure: I have zero affiliation with BlackLabel TCG — no partnership, no commission, nothing monetary changes hands between us in either direction, and this isn’t sponsored. Alex, who runs the place, is simply a great friend of mine, and the community he’s built there is one of the most welcoming I’ve come across. I just wanted more people to know about it.

About the place

BlackLabel TCG is a trading card shop and community hangout in Serangoon, run by Alex. It’s the kind of place where you pop in for singles and end up staying for hours because someone’s always up for a game or happy to talk cards.

Address: 50 Serangoon North Ave 4, #08-19 First Centre, Singapore 555856

Pokémon Gyms — come learn

They run official Pokémon Gym league nights every Friday and Saturday from 7pm. If you’re new and want to learn how to actually play, you can arrange to drop by — just reach out on their Telegram channel below and someone will sort you out. It’s a genuinely easy, friendly way to learn from people who know what they’re doing.

Terms & Conditions

The short version: this is a personal binder, not a store. Here’s exactly how it works.

No direct purchasing

This website has no direct purchasing capability — and that’s not a flaw, it’s designed this way on purpose. Jackson isn’t running an official business here; this simply serves as a digital binder so you can see what he currently has for sale.

How to buy something

Found something you want? Kindly click “Add to Poké Mart Cart” on the listing. Once you’re done browsing, go to your Poké Mart Cart and select “Contact Jack.” You can contact Jack via Telegram DMs, or by joining his Discord server and either DM-ing him privately or asking in the Pokémon text channel.

Once your message comes through, Jack will respond as soon as he can. Payment is made via PayNow or PayLah! — Jack will send over a QR code along with your final order amount and item list before you pay.

Jack has a day job and a young kid at home, so please be a little forgiving if he takes a bit longer than usual to reply — he’ll always get back to you.

Collection & mailing

Jack is based in Singapore, and can only hand over cards locally — there’s no international shipping at the moment. Once payment is confirmed, cards can be collected in person or mailed out:

  • Tampines MRT — specific days and timings only, DM Jack to discuss.
  • Upper Thomson MRT — Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, 2–7pm.
  • Mailing (SmartPac) — available for an additional $3. Multiple cards can share one SmartPac unless the order is too large.

Sending your list

The entire list of your cart, and its hyperlinks, should automatically be copied when you hit “Contact Jack” — simply paste it into the chat and he’ll respond as soon as he can.

Condition guide

Every card is graded honestly on this scale. Anything Moderately Played or below gets a written note under the listing explaining exactly where and how it’s worn.

M
Mint — flawless, pack-fresh.
NM
Near Mint — minimal to no wear.
LP
Lightly Played — minor edge/corner wear.
MP
Moderately Played — visible scratches or whitening.
HP
Heavily Played — heavy wear, possible small tears.
DMG
Damaged — bends, tears, writing, or similar.

Card flags explained

Some listings carry small badges for printing quirks that collectors look for. They’re not damage — they describe how the card came out of the factory.

Swirls
A galaxy-like swirl pattern in the holo foil, created during printing. Often sought after.
Holo Bleed
Holo foil extending slightly past the artwork window onto the border. A printing quirk some collectors prize.
Misprint
A factory error — miscut edges, off-centre printing, or ink irregularities.

About the photos

Thumbnail photos on this site are not an actual photo of the specific physical card and don’t represent its real condition. Please trust the condition, remarks, and any flags (swirls, holo bleed, misprint) stated on each individual listing. If you’d like real photos or more explanation about a specific card before committing, just message Jack — he’s happy to help.
